planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; twisted trillium grows on rich wooded slopes and ravine bottoms of Alabama, Mississippi, and Tennessee and is easy to identify by its distinctively twisted, horizontally spreading petals.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Twisted trillium is a sessile species of the mid-South, native to rich wooded slopes and ravines in Alabama, Mississippi, and Tennessee, named for its narrow maroon-purple petals, which spiral and twist as they spread out nearly horizontally above the mottled leaves rather than standing upright like most sessile trilliums. It blooms in early spring, with a faintly fetid scent typical of fly-pollinated trilliums, and its low, outstretched flower makes an eye-catching accent along a shaded woodland path where visitors can look down into the twisted petals. Give it the same rich, well-drained, humus-heavy soil favored by Trillium cuneatum, and avoid moving established clumps, since trillium rhizomes take years to recover fully from transplant.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in deep shade; persistent trillium is a federally threatened species restricted to a handful of gorge forests along the Tallulah and Chattooga Rivers in northeast Georgia and northwest South Carolina, and wild collection is illegal.

directions: Plant only nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in deep shade beneath rhododendron or mountain laurel, mimicking the steep gorge-forest understory where this species survives in the wild. Persistent trillium is a federally threatened pedicellate species known only from a small cluster of populations in the deep river gorges of the Tallulah and Chattooga watersheds in northeast Georgia and adjacent South Carolina, named for its narrow pink-to-white petals, which stay fresh and open far longer than those of most trilliums before fading. Because natural populations are so restricted and legally protected, it should be grown only from nursery-propagated stock as a specialty addition to a cool, deeply shaded woodland garden, never collected from the wild. It is slow to establish and slower still to reach flowering size, so patience and consistently cool, moist conditions are essential to success.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service — Species Profile
Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in deep shade under deciduous trees; Douglass's toothwort blooms earlier than the similar cutleaf toothwort and goes dormant by late spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the roots during summer garden work.

directions: Douglass's toothwort is one of the earliest eastern woodland spring ephemerals to bloom, often flowering while patches of snow still linger farther north, its clusters of pink to lavender-purple flowers opening on short stems above one or two broad, coarsely toothed leaves in rich, moist deciduous forest from the Appalachians west into the prairie states. It is readily told apart from the similar cutleaf toothwort by its deeper pink flower color, its broader and less finely divided leaves, and its slightly earlier bloom time, and the two species sometimes grow together in the same rich cove woods. Like other toothworts its knobby, tooth-shaped rhizomes have a mild horseradish bite and were traditionally eaten raw or added to salads. Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in deep shade; the plant sets seed and disappears completely by early summer, so pair it with later-emerging ferns or hostas to fill the gap.
